Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the vascular anatomy of the forearm, wrist, and hand and list clinically important
patterns and variations.
Describe and differentiate the pathophysiology of embolic and thrombotic conditions and
treatment options for each type of condition.
Explain the difference between aneurysm and pseudoaneurysm.
List the most common acute and chronic causes of vascular insufficiency of the upper
extremity.
Review Raynaud phenomenon and Raynaud disease and the various treatment options

Anatomy
The ulnar artery descends in the forearm deep to the flexor carpi ulnaris and is accompanied
in its course by the ulnar nerve (Figure 1).
Proximally, the ulnar artery gives off anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent branches.
The common interosseous artery arises from the proximal ulnar artery and divides into
anterior and posterior branches.
At the wrist, the dorsal branch of the ulnar artery originates 2 to 4 cm proximal to the
pisiform, travels below the abductor digiti minimi, and contributes to the deep palmar arch.
The ulnar artery proper enters the Guyon canal and passes into the palm and contributes to
the superficial palmar arch, which then courses radially.
The radial artery descends in the forearm deep to the brachioradialis and courses distally
between the flexor carpi radialis and brachioradialis.
At the wrist, the radial artery branches into a superficial palmar branch and a dorsal branch,
which courses in a dorsoradial direction to enter the anatomic snuffbox.
The dorsal branch travels between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle and
then divides to form the princeps pollicis and the deep palmar arch.
The superficial palmar arch is largely supplied by the ulnar artery.
Common branches include a deep branch to the deep palmar arch, the ulnar digital artery of
the small finger, and three common digital arteries.
The deep arch is formed by an anastomosis between the radial artery and the deep branch of
the ulnar artery.
Common branches include the princeps pollicis, the radialis indicis artery, and three palmar
metacarpal arteries.
A persistent median artery may accompany the median nerve in the carpal tunnel and reaches
the hand (palmar type).
The incidence is 4% to 23%.
A persistent median artery may contribute to median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel
and commonly is observed with a bifid median nerve.
The superficial or deep palmar arches are defined as complete if an anastomosis is present
between the vessels contributing to the arch.1
The deep arch is complete in 98% of individuals.
The superficial palmar arch is complete in 80% of individuals.
The radial artery alone or the ulnar artery alone generally is sufficient to provide arterial
supply to the hand in a normal healthy individual. In individuals with inadequate arterial inflow

and in whom arterial inflow is tenuous and requires contributions from the radial and ulnar
artery, ligation or removal or obstruction of one vessel may lead to ischemia.
This is clinically important because in acute traumatic events, one of the arteries occasionally
is ligated.
This is clinically important because the radial artery often is harvested for cardiac procedures
or used as an arterial line, which may result in injury.
The Allen test can be used to assess for a complete arch; however, its utility is questionable.
The concept of radial versus ulnar artery dominance refers to the concept that one of the
vessels is the primary contributor to vascular inflow. The literature is conflicting on the artery
that most commonly is dominant; variability likely exists among individuals.2

Pathophysiology
Ischemia is caused by vasospasm and/or occlusion.
Vasospasm is the result of increased sympathetic tone.3
Occlusion is the result of embolism, thrombosis, stenosis, or aneurysm.
Clinical Evaluation and Diagnostic Studies
The modified Allen test involves holding firm, occlusive pressure on the radial artery and the
ulnar artery. The patient is asked to clench the fist several times until the palmar skin is
blanched. The patient then opens the hand, and pressure on the ulnar artery is released while
occlusion of the radial artery is maintained. The time required for palmar capillary refill is
noted. The test is then repeated, and the radial artery is released while the ulnar artery
remains compressed (Video 1).
Video 1 Seiler JG III: Physical examination of the hand and wrist: Thumb CMC arthritis tests.
Allen test, in Sarwark JF, ed: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American

Handheld pencil Doppler is a simple, accurate, and noninvasive method that can be used to
evaluate perfusion.
Pulse oximetry is widely available and offers an objective assessment of tissue perfusion via
assessment of oxygenation.
Arterial duplex imaging provides dynamic information regarding flow, vessel compliance, and
turbulence.
Digital plethysmography (pulse volume recordings) quantifies flow via changes in digit
volume and demonstrates compliance and perfusion via tracings.
Digital brachial indices (DBIs) allow for quantification of relative blood flow.4
DBI is calculated by dividing digital blood pressure by brachial blood pressure.
A DBI greater than 0.7 suggests adequate blood flow.
Angiography is the preferred method for diagnosing vascular disorders of the hand and
wrist.
Vascular Occlusive Disease
Ulnar Artery Thrombosis (Hypothenar Hammer Syndrome)
General information
Ulnar artery thrombosis is the most common vascular occlusive disease of the upper
extremity.
The condition was initially described in 1934 by von Rosen.
Conn coined the term hypothenar hammer syndrome, indicating the pathophysiology was
commonly observed in patients who used the ulnar aspect of the hand as a tool for
impaction.
Most commonly diagnosed in male laborers in their forties or fifties
Prevalence in industrial workers ranges from 7% to 14%.
Pathophysiology
The ulnar side of the hand strikes an object, causing the pisiform to deviate radially into the
Guyon canal.
In turn, the ulnar artery is believed to be at risk for compression against the hook of the
hamate.

Repetitive trauma is believed to lead to periadventitial thickening or disruption of internal
elastic lamina.
Periadventitial thickening and continued intimal damage is thought to result in aneurysmal
dilation with mural thrombi, variable occlusion, and distal embolic events.
Patient presentation
Symptoms include cold intolerance, pain, cyanosis, ulceration, and sensory dysfunction
(decreased sensation and sweating), typically observed in the more ulnar digits.
Signs include the following:
Presence of a pulsatile mass
Trophic changes in the ulnar digits, including ulceration and change in turgor
Decreased ulnar sensibility
Absent or slow filling through the ulnar artery via the Allen test
Diagnostic testing
Duplex ultrasonography
Digital pressures and pulse volume recording
CT/magnetic resonance angiography
Digital subtraction angiography (Figure 2)
Figure 2 Arteriogram of a right hand shows ulnar artery thrombosis (between asterisks).

Management5
Nonsurgical or medical management may include the following:
Avoid using the hand as a hammer
Smoking cessation
Calcium channel blockers or beta blockers
Phosphodiesterase inhibitors
Surgical treatment is considered in patients with digital ulceration/necrosis or rest pain.6
Ligation
Leriche sympathectomy
Indicated with DBI higher than 0.7
Resection and autologous vascular reconstruction
Vein graft (ie, saphenous) versus arterial graft (ie, medial femoral circumflex)
Indicated with DBI lower than 0.7
Even if initial flow at time of reconstruction is satisfactory, a high rate of re-occlusion has
been reported, which does not appear to affect outcomes7 (Resources 1 and 2).
Embolic Disease
General
Common sources of upper extremity emboli are the heart (most common), subclavian artery,
and superficial palmar arch.
70% of upper extremity emboli are of cardiac origin.
Conditions predisposing patients to emboli include atrial fibrillation, thoracic outlet
narrowing, prothrombotic conditions, and recent surgical thrombectomy.
Diagnosis
Patient history will reveal an acute episode of pain.
Physical examination findings include pallor, petechiae, and absent pulses.
Echocardiography and arteriography may aid in the localization of the source of the emboli.
Management

period, typically followed by anticoagulation for 3 months or more.
Intravenous thrombolytic agents8
Catheter-directed thrombectomy and/or thrombolytics
Aneurysms and Pseudoaneurysms
Aneurysm
General
A true aneurysm is composed of all layers in the vessel wall.
The ulnar artery is the artery most commonly affected in the upper extremity.
Risk factors
Blunt trauma
Atherosclerosis
Infection
Autoimmune
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Patient presentation
Patients present with an enlarging pulsatile mass
Patients may present with paresthesias, pain, and occasional ischemia or other trophic
changes
Diagnosis
Allen test
Colored Doppler ultrasonography
Angiography
Management
Arterial ligation with aneurysm excision
Excision with end-to-end repair
Excision with autologous reconstruction
Pseudoaneurysm
General
Pseudoaneurysms are caused by penetrating trauma to the intima of the artery.

Pseudoaneurysms result from recanalized hematoma and do not contain any layer of the
vessel wall. Instead, they form a fibrous eccentric evagination that communicates with the
arterial lumen.
Risk factors
Cardiac catheterization
Arterial line monitoring
Penetrating wound
Systemic anticoagulation therapy
Patient presentation
Patients present with a painless, pulsatile mass.
Diagnosis
Duplex ultrasonography
Angiography
Management depends on the location and presence of good collateral circulation.9
Treatment options include the following:
Observation with spontaneous resolution
Nonsurgical management with compression
Excision and vessel ligation (Figure 3 )
Excision and primary repair
Excision with vein or patch grafting

Buerger Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans)
General
Buerger disease is a nonatherosclerotic condition characterized by recurring progressive
inflammation, with stenosis and thrombus in small and medium-sized vessels of the hands
and feet10
Disease is more severe peripherally.
Risk Factors
Buerger disease occurs almost exclusively in young men (aged 40 to 45 years) who use
tobacco.
Hereditary susceptibility

Infectious etiology (Rickettsia)
Patient Presentation
Severe pain at rest and cold intolerance
Raynaud phenomenon
Trophic changes that may evolve to include digital ischemia and necrosis
Diagnosis
Shionoya criteria: history of smoking, onset of symptoms before age 50 years, infrapopliteal
arterial occlusions, upper extremity involvement, and absence of other atherosclerotic risk
factors.
Diagnosis is made via histology.
Acute phase: cellular, segmental, occlusive inflammatory thrombi with relative sparing of the
blood-vessel wall
Subacute phase: progressive organization of the thrombus in the arteries and veins
End stage: mature thrombi and vascular fibrosis
Management/Therapy
Smoking cessation slows disease progression and is the mainstay of management.11
Intravenous iloprost is more effective than aspirin for eradicating rest pain and healing
ischemic ulcers.
Amputation is reserved for recalcitrant nonhealing wounds or nonviable digits after cessation
of smoking.
Vasospastic Disease of the Hand
General
Most causes of vasospastic disease are unknown.5,7
Raynaud disease and phenomenon are clinical conditions associated with vasospasm.
Raynaud described the phenomenon of vascular spasm, with eventual gangrene in the
extremities related to the sympathetic nervous system (Figure 4).

Raynaud disease is idiopathic, with symptoms of reduced peripheral circulation. Irreversible
tissue injury does not result from the condition.
Raynaud phenomenon occurs in patients with a collagen vascular disease, particularly
scleroderma. It is a progressive condition characterized by digital trophic changes, an
abnormal Allen test, asymmetric findings, and abnormal angiography.5
Patients typically present with episodic color changes of the extremities in response to cold
exposure or to emotional stress. The finger characteristically turns white (representing
vasospasm), then blue (deoxygenation), and ultimately red (indicating reperfusion
hyperemia).
Figure 4 Medial (A) and palmar (B) view clinical photographs of bilateral hands show dry
gangrenous changes. (Reproduced with permission from Ejiyooye TF, Ajibowo AO, Dirisanala S,
Olagbende B, Ezenagu UE, Khan A: A rare case of thromboangiitis obliterans of bilateral upper
extremities in an adult male. Cureus 2022;14[5]:e24975.)
Raynaud Disease
Generally affects otherwise healthy women before age 30 years
Prevalence near 10% in women and 8% in men.
Multiple mechanisms for the development of symptoms have been proposed.12
Reduced endothelin-dependent vasodilation
Reduction of the immunoreactivity of calcitonin gene-related peptide
Overproduction of endothelin-1
Management
Avoidance of cold stimuli

Keeping the extremities warm with additional clothing, such as gloves, insulated drinking
containers, and hand warmers
Calcium channel blockers
Raynaud Phenomenon
Occurs in patients with connective tissue disease (eg, scleroderma)
Pathophysiology13
Hyperactivity of the sympathetic nervous system
Increased levels of endothelin
Enhanced platelet aggregation
Red blood cell deformability
Patient presentation
Digital trophic changes
Asymmetric findings
Diagnosis
Detailed patient history and physical examination evaluating for signs of connective tissue
disease
Abnormal Allen test
Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-
reactive protein level, and antinuclear antibody test
Nailfold capillaroscopy (Figure 5)
Arteriography can rule out occlusive or embolic disease.
Management/Therapy14
Avoidance of cold exposure and stress management improves vasospastic symptoms.
Rheumatology referral for systemic management
Smoking cessation and discontinuation of sympathomimetic drugs
Calcium channel blockers diminish vasoconstriction.
Transdermal nitrates mimic the vasodilator and protective activity of endothelium-derived
nitric oxide.
Other agents include phosphodiesterase inhibitors (eg, Sildenafil or tadalafil), antiplatelet
therapy, prostanoids, or endothelin-1 inhibitors.
Botulinum toxin injections (believed to paralyze smooth muscle of vessel wall)
Surgical sympathectomy is used for recalcitrant cases.
